Covenant is a big word and assumes a solemn promise 
made binding by oath which may be expressed either by a 
verbal formula or symbolic action. Such an action or for^ 
mula is recognised by both parties as the formal act which 
binds the actor to fulfil his promise. Covenants may be esta- 
blished between parties of different socio-political groups or 
within a legal community. Covenant usually had sanction 
of a religious nature, and as such it was closely connected 
with religion. The poet deals only with the more pertinent 
aspects of the covenant. Hence the suggestion of the title. 

In this poem God is not a party to the covenant since 
God acts in his freedom-Covenant is a free gift of God and 
is offered to any person wishing to abide by it. Its value

can bo anticipated m terms of man’s participation in the 
mission of God to the world. Deep down the heart of man 
there is a craving for involvement in the covenant because co- 
venant is the only way by which man can reach upto God. 
The way is paved by various obstacles but in the end after a 
long and perilous pilgrimage man reaches the haven of peace 
and tranquility stripped of all his vanity and pride and all 
the worldly cares and anxieties purified by the sense of parti- 
cipation in the covenant. 

The poet gives the impression of being influenced by 
some of the lofty and noble thoughts found in Rabindranath 
Tagore’s Gita^jali, Psalms, the Book of Job, Milton’s 
Paradise Lost and John Banyan’s Pilgrim Progress. 

Stanza 165 **To my hearth and home I shall return 

far far away from the World with many faces” 
reminds us of Gitangli **Into that haven of 
peace my Father let my country awake’* 



ii 


Stanza 1 16 ‘^Tbou also causeth my vessel to overflow with 
the living water” is reminiscent of ^alm 23 
“my cup overflows.” 

The poem is written in free verse. There is generally no 
break of thought between the first, second and subsequent 
stanzas and this keeps the interest of the reader to the end. 
Between lines are interspersed with rich imaginaries drawn 
from the beautiful nature and real life.

Some of the defects may be pointed out. 

Between the various parts, the poem contains passages 
of great beauty. These are little “short swallow flights of 
song” On the whole the poem seems to suffer from lack of 
organic unity, and from so newhat u leasy wavering between 
jest and earnest in the matter of treatment but it is signifi* 
cant of the trend of the poet’s mind in the direction of cur- 
rent thought. Here and there the highly wrought craftsman- 
ship obtrudes a shade too much and passes the line between 
art and artificiality; but the lapses are few, and the inevita 
ble expressions many.
